chapter_summary:
Welcome to the crucial world of Requirements Engineering! This phase is the bedrock of any successful software project. Think of it like an architect designing a building: before any bricks are laid, they need to understand exactly what the client wants – how many rooms, what style, what materials, and what purpose the building will serve. In software, these "wants" and "needs" are what we call *requirements*. Requirements Engineering is the systematic process of discovering, documenting, analyzing, validating, and managing these requirements throughout the software development lifecycle. It's not just about writing down a list of features; it's about truly understanding the problem we're trying to solve and defining the solution clearly.

The importance of robust requirements engineering cannot be overstated. Studies consistently show that a significant percentage of project failures can be attributed to poor requirements – misunderstandings, ambiguities, or incomplete specifications. Imagine building a complex system only to find out halfway through that it doesn't meet the users' actual needs, or that a critical feature was overlooked. Fixing errors late in the development cycle, especially after deployment, is exponentially more expensive and time-consuming than addressing them during the initial requirements phase. This is often referred to as the "cost of change" curve, where the cost of fixing a defect rises dramatically the later it is discovered. By investing time and effort upfront, we mitigate risks, reduce rework, and ensure the final product aligns with stakeholder expectations.

Requirements typically fall into two main categories: functional and non-functional. **Functional requirements** describe *what* the system must *do*. These are the core features and behaviors of the software. For an e-commerce website, functional requirements might include: "The system shall allow users to browse products by category," "The system shall allow users to add items to a shopping cart," or "The system shall process credit card payments securely." They directly relate to the user's interaction with the system and its core business logic. These are often expressed as actions or capabilities of the system.

On the other hand, **non-functional requirements (NFRs)** describe *how well* the system performs its functions, or the qualities and constraints under which it operates. These often dictate the system's overall user experience and operational characteristics. Examples of NFRs include performance (e.g., "The system shall load product pages within 2 seconds"), security (e.g., "The system shall encrypt all user passwords"), usability (e.g., "The user interface shall be intuitive for first-time users"), reliability (e.g., "The system shall be available 99.9% of the time"), scalability, maintainability, and portability. While functional requirements define the "what," non-functional requirements define the "quality attributes" or "constraints" that shape the system's design and architecture. Ignoring NFRs can lead to a system that works but is slow, insecure, or difficult to use, ultimately failing to satisfy its users.

Effective requirements engineering also heavily relies on identifying and engaging the right **stakeholders**. Stakeholders are anyone with an interest in or influence over the project, or who will be affected by the system. This includes end-users, business owners, project managers, developers, testers, legal teams, and even regulatory bodies. Each stakeholder group brings a unique perspective and set of needs. For instance, a marketing manager might prioritize features that enhance customer engagement, while a system administrator will focus on ease of deployment and maintenance. A common mistake is to only involve a subset of stakeholders, leading to an incomplete or biased understanding of the requirements. It's crucial to cast a wide net and ensure diverse voices are heard and their needs are considered. Understanding these different perspectives is key to building a comprehensive and well-rounded set of requirements that truly reflect the project's objectives.

screens.title: Introduction to Requirements Engineering
screens.subtitle: Why clear requirements are the foundation of every successful software project

narration.text: Welcome. In this lesson you will explore requirements engineering, the practice of discovering, documenting, analyzing, validating, and managing what software must do and how well it must perform. Think of an architect creating a building blueprint: without a clear plan you risk costly rework later. Requirements engineering helps teams avoid that risk by turning stakeholder needs into clear, testable statements. We'll use practical examples such as an online library and an e-commerce feature to show the difference between functional requirements — what the system must do — and non-functional requirements — the qualities that shape how the system behaves. You will also learn who to involve: end users, business owners, developers, testers, administrators, and regulatory stakeholders. Finally, we will look at the consequences of vague requirements and how early validation reduces the cost of change. By the end of this module you will be able to write concise requirements, spot ambiguous statements, and explain why early stakeholder engagement matters. Consider: what small detail, if missing, could break your next project?

narration.text: In this first objectives slide we'll set clear targets. You will learn to define requirements engineering in precise, practical terms so you can explain its role in reducing late project changes. You will also learn to distinguish functional requirements — statements of behaviour or capabilities — from non-functional requirements that specify qualities like performance or security. Each objective links a concrete skill to why that skill matters: for example, writing a testable functional requirement prevents ambiguous interpretations by developers and testers. We will also introduce stakeholder identification; knowing who to involve prevents missing critical needs and reduces rework. Finally, you'll learn to recognize the real cost of poorly defined requirements so you can advocate for early discovery and validation. Each card below explains the competency, gives a small mnemonic, and points to the verified competency milestone you can aim for. Keep these objectives in mind as checkpoints while you work through the lesson examples and the hands-on library task.

screens.title: What is Requirements Engineering?
screens.subtitle: A systematic approach to capturing needs and constraints

narration.text: Requirements engineering is the set of activities that lets a team move from vague ideas to clear, usable specifications. At its heart are five activities: discover what stakeholders need, document that need as clear statements, analyze for conflicts and completeness, validate the statements against real users or prototypes, and manage changes over time. Think of an architect who interviews a client, draws plans, checks the design with the client, and then tracks changes as construction proceeds. A useful concrete example is an online library: discovery might reveal that users want to search by author and ISBN; documentation records a requirement like "The system shall allow users to search books by title, author, or ISBN." Analysis checks for conflicts such as two stakeholders requesting mutually exclusive behaviour. Validation uses walkthroughs or simple prototypes so stakeholders can react. Managing requirements means tracking updates, knowing why a change was made, and ensuring tests and design follow the latest requirement. A common misconception is to treat requirements as a static list; the reality is they evolve and require active governance. The takeaway is simple: treat requirements as living artifacts that guide design and testing, not as a one-time checklist.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Requirements engineering converts stakeholder needs into living, verifiable specifications through discovery, documentation, analysis, validation, and management.

screens.title: The Requirements Engineering Process
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step workflow from discovery to management

narration.text: The requirements engineering process can be framed as a repeatable flow: discover, document, analyze, validate, and manage. Discovery is gathering needs through interviews, observations, and stakeholder workshops. For example, in the library scenario you might observe users searching for books and note frustrations with broad search results. Documentation turns those findings into concise, testable statements. A good documentation habit is to write requirements in a consistent template such as "The system shall..." which makes acceptance criteria easier to define. Analysis looks for conflicts, duplicates, and missing pieces — for example, two stakeholders may request different default sorting behaviours. Validation is where you check assumptions with stakeholders: run a walkthrough, build a quick prototype, or define acceptance tests to prove a requirement is met. Finally, management tracks changes and ensures traceability: every requirement should map to tests and design items and record why it changed. A common mistake is skipping validation; teams often assume a written requirement is understood. The result is fewer surprises and lower cost of change when you treat this flow as iterative and evidence-driven. The Requirements Engineering Process means follow a cycle of discovery, documentation, analysis, validation, and management to reduce ambiguity and support traceability.. In practical terms, a step-by-step workflow from discovery to management. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Process
keyIdea.text: Follow a cycle of discovery, documentation, analysis, validation, and management to reduce ambiguity and support traceability.

Five-step flow
Repeatable and iterative
1. Discover
Gather stakeholder needs through interviews and observation. Example: watch users search the catalog to see real problems.
2. Document
Write concise, testable statements such as "The system shall..." to make acceptance criteria clear.
3. Analyze
Find conflicts or missing requirements, and resolve priority or scope issues with stakeholders.
4. Validate

5. Manage

Concrete scenario
Discovery note

Documented requirement

The system shall allow users to filter search results by ISBN and publication year.

Validation approach

Create a clickable prototype and ask five representative users to search by ISBN.

Key Takeaway

Make discovery and validation explicit steps. Testing assumptions early saves time and money.

screens.title: Importance and the Cost of Change
screens.subtitle: Why early requirements work reduces expensive fixes later

narration.text: One of the strongest arguments for good requirements engineering is the cost of change. As a project progresses, the cost and effort to correct a misunderstanding typically increase. Early in the lifecycle, clarifying a requirement may take a conversation and a small document update. Later, the same fix can require code changes, regression testing, deployment, and user retraining — each multiplies cost. Imagine discovering that a search function was supposed to filter by ISBN only after launch; rolling back, changing interfaces, and fixing data handling can be time consuming. The practical result is that investing effort in discovery, clear documentation, and validation early reduces overall project cost and risk. That said, another misconception is to over-document when quick prototypes would reveal the same insights faster. The balance is to capture enough detail to build and test while validating assumptions with users. Ask yourself: what assumption, if false, would cause the largest rework, and how can you validate that assumption early? Importance and the Cost of Change means fixing requirement errors early costs far less than correcting them after design or deployment; validation reduces risk and budget waste.. In practical terms, why early requirements work reduces expensive fixes later. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Cost of Change Curve
Early validation reduces expensive fixes
Illustrative timeline
Discovery phase — low cost to change: conversations and small edits.
Design & implementation — higher cost: code changes and regression tests.
Deployment & maintenance — highest cost: patches, data migration, user impact.
Example

screens.title: Functional Requirements — The 'What'
screens.subtitle: Clear statements of system behaviour with concrete examples

narration.text: Functional requirements describe what the system must do. They are action-oriented statements about features and behaviours that users expect. For an e-commerce site these include actions like browsing products, adding items to a shopping cart, or processing payments. For our online library example, functional requirements would include searching for books, viewing detailed metadata, checking out and returning books, and managing hold queues. A helpful way to write them is to use a consistent phrasing such as "The system shall..." which makes the intended behaviour explicit and easier to test. Concrete examples reduce ambiguity: instead of saying "search should be good," write "The system shall allow users to search by title, author, or ISBN and return results within the current catalog." A common misconception is conflating implementation detail with a requirement; a requirement should state the need, not how to implement it. The takeaway is to keep functional requirements focused, measurable, and described in terms of observable system behaviour. Functional Requirements — The 'What' means functional requirements state the observable behaviours and features the system must provide and should be written to be testable.. In practical terms, clear statements of system behaviour with concrete examples. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Functional
keyIdea.text: Functional requirements state the observable behaviours and features the system must provide and should be written to be testable.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Functional Requirements
Functional requirements
Statements of behaviour the system must provide
Good example
The system shall allow users to search books by title, author, or ISBN.
The system shall allow users to check out and return books using their library account.
The system shall show book availability status and estimated return dates.
Misconception
Avoid embedding implementation details such as specific database queries in the requirement.
Key Takeaway

Write functional requirements as observable behaviour in a consistent, testable format.

Concrete scenario
A user searches by ISBN and the system returns the exact match with availability. This is a functional requirement because it describes behaviour.
Example checklist
  • Is the statement measurable? Yes: searchable fields are enumerated.
  • Can a tester verify it? Yes: provide ISBN and check result.
  • Does it avoid implementation details? Yes.

screens.title: Non-Functional Requirements — The 'How Well'
screens.subtitle: Quality attributes and constraints that shape the system

narration.text: Non-functional requirements describe qualities, constraints, and expectations for how the system performs and behaves rather than specific features. Common categories include performance, security, usability, reliability, scalability, maintainability, and portability. For example, a performance NFR might state that product pages must load within two seconds under typical load. A security NFR could require encryption of user passwords or secure transmission of financial data. A usability NFR might require the interface to be intuitive for first-time users. Non-functional requirements shape architecture and design choices: performance influences caching and database design, security shapes authentication and encryption, and scalability affects how you design for growth. A frequent mistake is to leave NFRs implicit; this results in a system that may function but fails on user expectation or operational constraints. When writing NFRs, prefer measurable targets like response time, availability percentage, or maximum acceptable downtime. The takeaway is to treat NFRs as first-class requirements because they determine the system’s real-world success. Non-Functional Requirements — The 'How Well' means nfrs set measurable quality targets and constraints — treat them as first-class requirements to guide architecture and testing.. In practical terms, quality attributes and constraints that shape the system. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Non-functional
keyIdea.text: NFRs set measurable quality targets and constraints — treat them as first-class requirements to guide architecture and testing.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Non-Functional Requirements
Non-functional requirements
Quality attributes and constraints
Performance
Example: product pages shall load within 2 seconds under typical load.
Security
Example: encrypt user passwords and use secure transmission for financial data.
Usability
Example: new users should complete checkout within three clicks on first attempt.
Reliability & Availability
Example: the system shall be available 99.9% of the time.
Key Takeaway

Give non-functional requirements measurable targets so architects and testers can confirm them.

Example — Library NFRs
Performance
Search results return within 2 seconds for catalogs under 50,000 items.
Security
User passwords must be stored using one-way hashing; communications must be encrypted.
Usability
First-time users must find and borrow a book within three minutes without external help.

screens.title: Functional vs Non-Functional — Side-by-side
screens.subtitle: How to tell the difference and avoid confusion

narration.text: Distinguishing functional from non-functional requirements is essential because they drive different design conversations. Functional requirements focus on specific actions such as "search by title" or "checkout a book." They are verified by executing the action and checking the result. Non-functional requirements focus on qualities — response time, security, usability — and are verified by performance tests, security reviews, or usability testing. A common confusion is to write a quality inside a functional statement or vice versa. For example, "The search shall be fast" is vague; better is to separate: a functional requirement "The system shall support search by title, author, or ISBN." paired with an NFR "Search results shall return within 2 seconds under typical load." This separation helps teams decide whether they need a UI change, an algorithm improvement, or infrastructure scaling. A typical misconception is to assume performance will 'come for free'; in reality, performance targets influence architecture. The closing question: which requirements in your project belong to which category, and how will you test each? Functional vs Non-Functional — Side-by-side means functional requirements define actions to perform; non-functional requirements define measurable qualities and constraints to be tested differently.. In practical terms, how to tell the difference and avoid confusion. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Contrast
keyIdea.text: Functional requirements define actions to perform; non-functional requirements define measurable qualities and constraints to be tested differently.

Functional

screens.title: Stakeholders and Their Perspectives
screens.subtitle: Who to involve and what each group cares about

narration.text: Stakeholders are anyone with an interest in the project or who will be affected by the system. Typical groups include end-users, business owners, product managers, developers, testers, system administrators, legal or compliance teams, and external regulators. Each brings a different priority: users emphasise ease of use and relevant features, business owners focus on value and market fit, developers look for clarity and feasibility, and administrators care about deployment and maintenance. If you only consult one group, you risk biased requirements that miss operational or compliance constraints. For example, a marketing manager may request features that increase engagement, while a system administrator may insist on maintainability and deployment simplicity. A practical approach is to map stakeholders, identify their primary concerns, and ensure representative voices are included in discovery and validation. A common misconception is that developers can infer user needs; while developers can propose solutions, direct input from users avoids assumptions. The takeaway: cast a wide net early and confirm each stakeholder's top priorities so requirements reflect a balanced view. Stakeholders and Their Perspectives means identify and include all groups affected by the system to capture diverse needs and avoid biased requirements.. In practical terms, who to involve and what each group cares about. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Stakeholder mapping
Identify who matters and why

Operations & Admin

Key Takeaway

Map stakeholders early, include diverse voices during discovery, and validate requirements with representatives from each group.

screens.title: Validation and Managing Requirements
screens.subtitle: How to confirm requirements and keep them current

narration.text: Validation and active management are the glue that keeps requirements useful. Validation confirms the requirement actually reflects stakeholder needs; common techniques include walkthroughs, prototypes, acceptance criteria, and simple tests that stakeholders can observe. For example, present a prototype search flow to users and ask them to complete a set of tasks; observing failures reveals ambiguous or missing requirements. Managing requirements means recording changes, linking each requirement to tests and design work, and keeping a clear history of why a change occurred. This traceability helps when a new stakeholder requests a change — you can assess impact on tests and design. A common misconception is that a signed requirements document eliminates the need for ongoing validation; in reality, changes in business priorities or environment still require re-validation. In practice, keep requirements concise, pair them with acceptance criteria, and maintain a simple change log so teams can safely adapt without losing alignment. Validation and Managing Requirements means validate with prototypes or acceptance criteria and manage changes with traceability to tests and design for safe, controlled evolution.. In practical terms, how to confirm requirements and keep them current. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Online Library
screens.subtitle: Identify functional and non-functional requirements for a simple library system

narration.text: Let's apply learning with a short, practical activity. You are building an online library where users can search for books, view details, and check out or return books. Start by listing at least three functional requirements that directly describe behaviour. Examples could include: "The system shall allow users to search by title, author, or ISBN," "The system shall allow users to check out books to their account," and "The system shall display book availability and due date when a title is selected." Next, list three non-functional requirements that set quality expectations, such as performance, security, or usability. Examples: "Search queries shall return results within two seconds under typical load," "User passwords must be encrypted in storage," and "First-time users shall complete a checkout within three minutes without assistance." When you write these, make them measurable and avoid implementation details. A common mistake is to write vague NFRs like "the system shall be fast" — instead specify a measurable threshold. After writing the requirements, pair each with one acceptance criterion to make testing straightforward. The skill here is turning observations into clear, testable statements.

keyIdea.title: Activity
keyIdea.text: Practice writing three functional and three non-functional, measurable requirements for an online library and add acceptance criteria for each.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › Hands-on Activity: Online Library
Activity: define requirements
Write three functional and three non-functional requirements with acceptance criteria
Functional requirements (examples)
1. The system shall allow users to search books by title, author, or ISBN.
   Acceptance: Given a valid title or ISBN, search returns matching results.
2. The system shall allow users to check out books to their account.
   Acceptance: After checkout, the book appears in the user's loans and availability decreases.
3. The system shall display book availability and estimated return date.
   Acceptance: Selecting a book shows current availability and the next due date if borrowed.
Non-functional requirements (examples)
1. Performance: Search results shall return within 2 seconds under typical load.
   Acceptance: Performance test shows median response ≤ 2s for representative queries.
2. Security: User passwords shall be stored using one-way hashing and all transmission encrypted.
   Acceptance: Security review confirms hashed storage and encrypted transport.
3. Usability: First-time users shall complete a checkout within 3 minutes without assistance.
   Acceptance: Usability test with representative learners confirms the metric.
Tip
Pair each requirement with an acceptance criterion to make testing and validation straightforward.

screens.title: Consequences of Poor Requirements and Sample Assessment
screens.subtitle: What goes wrong when requirements are vague and how to check understanding

narration.text: Poorly defined requirements cause a range of problems: scope creep, rework, missed user needs, increased cost, schedule overruns, and systems that technically work but fail to satisfy users. When requirements are ambiguous, developers make assumptions that may not match business needs; when stakeholders are missing, important constraints like compliance or maintenance requirements can be omitted. Fixing these kinds of mistakes late is expensive because it often requires changes across code, tests, and deployment scripts, and it can erode stakeholder trust. To assess understanding, consider the sample multiple-choice question from the chapter: which is a non-functional requirement? The correct answer is the option specifying encryption during transmission, because it describes a quality attribute (security) rather than a behaviour. Also ask: why is involving diverse stakeholders early important? The answer is it captures different priorities — users, business, operations — reducing omissions and conflicts. A practical check: review three requirements and ask whether each is testable, who verifies it, and what acceptance criteria prove it. screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's review the most important ideas to take forward. First, requirements engineering is the structured practice of discovering, documenting, analyzing, validating, and managing requirements so software meets stakeholder needs. Second, functional requirements state what the system must do; they should be observable and testable. Third, non-functional requirements describe qualities and constraints such as performance, security, and usability, and must include measurable targets. Fourth, stakeholder identification and engagement is essential: diverse perspectives prevent omissions and conflicting priorities. Finally, because the cost to fix errors rises sharply later in development, validating assumptions early with prototypes or acceptance criteria saves time and money. Keep these concepts visible as you write and review requirements; they will help you produce clearer, testable specifications and build better systems. screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to use every day

narration.text: A final quick reference to keep in mind: first, always make requirements testable and measurable so verification is straightforward. Second, separate functional statements (what) from non-functional statements (how well) and give NFRs concrete targets. Third, involve diverse stakeholders early and validate requirements with prototypes or acceptance criteria to reduce costly misunderstandings. Use these reminders as a checklist when you write or review requirements: is it testable, is the category clear, and have you validated it with a stakeholder? These three checks will help you catch the most common errors early and keep the project aligned.
